kurz: Why most flattering return figures arise without any intent and how seven check questions can expose them within a few minutes.

bloecke.md:
Every return figure is a statement about a sample. How this sample is put together helps to determine the result, often more strongly than the market it is supposed to measure. It almost always comes down to three points: who is included in the data and who is missing, where the start and end of the period lie, and whether the rule was set before or after the data.

None of these points implies fraud. Most inflated figures arise without any intent, because the most convenient data source also produces the most favourable picture.

## Closed and merged funds

A fund with a weak track record is rarely closed. More often, it is merged into a better-performing fund of the same company. Mergers of segregated fund assets (Sondervermögen) are governed by Sections 181 et seq. KAGB (German Investment Code), and liquidation by Section 99 KAGB. Both are legally permissible and often sensible from a cost perspective. For the data, however, this has a clear consequence. The history of the merged fund disappears from current databases, while that of the absorbing fund is continued. Only the funds that have survived remain.

S&P Dow Jones Indices also measures the extent of this thinning out in the SPIVA scorecards. Of the active US equity funds that existed in mid-2005, 37.3% still existed twenty years later. Over fifteen years the figure was 50.9%, over ten years 63.8%. In Europe, 58% of equity funds and 54% of bond funds survived over ten years. In the first half of 2025 alone, 2.4% of European equity funds were closed or merged. [[Survivorship bias]] is therefore not a marginal effect. In almost every fund statistic, it is the largest single distortion.

bloecke.titel: Survival rate of active US equity funds by period
bloecke.unter: After twenty years, just over a third of the funds that existed at the start are still in existence. Analyses that look only at today's funds leave the rest out of account.

bloecke.md:
At the start of the twenty-year period, there were 2,373 active US equity funds. At the end, 885 of them still existed. The remaining 1,488 had been closed or merged.

A league table that today shows the twenty-year return of “all funds” therefore contains 885 funds and no information on the other 1,488. It is correctly calculated, but it answers a different question from the one the reader is asking.

Reputable analyses state the survival rate explicitly and include closed funds in the result instead of deleting them. If there is no information at all on the population at the start of the period, the figure is systematically biased upwards. This applies to fund rankings, to portfolio comparisons on social trading platforms and to any statistic on the returns of strategies that users can create and delete themselves.

## Back-calculated index histories

An index launched in 2019 can be back-calculated to 1999 using the same rules. This is permitted and is labelled, because every index factsheet states a launch date and a data start date. Between the data start date and the launch date lies simulated history. It differs from real history in that the designer already knew the data when setting the rule. Article 13 of the Benchmarks Regulation (EU) 2016/1011 requires index providers to disclose their methodology. This makes the final rule traceable, but not the number of discarded earlier versions.

Huang, Song and Xiang measured the size of this difference in 2023 in the Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis. In retrospect, smart beta indices achieved an excess return of around three percentage points a year before the launch of the associated ETF. Afterwards, the excess return was minus 0.5% to minus 1%. The authors attribute this to selection in the index construction itself and not to capacity limits or poor timing.

For advertising in Germany, Article 44 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565 applies directly. Past performance must be shown for at least five years in twelve-month periods, with the source, a currency notice and a warning. Simulated performance may be shown only under strict conditions and clearly labelled. The rule prevents people from being misled about whether a figure is real or simulated, but it does not prevent the figure itself from being flattered.

bloecke.titel: Excess return of smart beta indices before and after product launch
bloecke.unter: Excess return over the market in percentage points a year, according to Huang/Song/Xiang 2023. For the period after launch, the study gives a range of −0.5 to −1; the midpoint is shown.

bloecke.md: The back-calculation becomes a real problem as soon as more than one variant is tested. Every threshold, every rebalancing interval and every filter is a parameter, and every combination is another attempt. In 2014, Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado and Zhu showed in the *Notices of the American Mathematical Society* how quickly spurious results arise in this way. With a few dozen variants on five years of data, one with a Sharpe ratio of around 1 will very probably be found, purely through random fluctuations and without any effect in the data. The minimum length a backtest needs grows with the logarithm of the number of attempts. Yet almost always only the best variant is published, and almost never the number of attempts.

## Using information that came later

A [[look-ahead bias]] arises when a test uses information that was not yet public at the time of trading. The most common form concerns timing. Balance sheet data are dated to the balance sheet date instead of the day of their publication. Under Section 114(1) WpHG (Securities Trading Act), issuers have four months to publish the annual financial report.

The second form concerns composition. A back-calculation of today's forty DAX stocks to 1988 tests a portfolio of companies that have survived to this day. Wirecard was a DAX member from September 2018 to August 2020 and filed for insolvency in June 2020. In such a back-calculation, the company does not appear. The same error is found in every test that holds “the 500 stocks of the S&P 500” over decades without reconstructing historical index membership.

bloecke.titel: A backtest that cannot be traded
bloecke.md:
A strategy buys the twenty shares with the lowest price-to-earnings ratio every year on 2 January, calculated from the accounts as of 31 December. In hindsight, this works very well.

On 2 January, however, these accounts were not yet available anywhere. The test therefore buys using figures that only appeared in March or April, and thereby favours companies whose financial year turned out to be good with hindsight.

Fama and French therefore leave a gap of six months between the balance sheet date and portfolio formation in their factor data. When reading a backtest, you should look for this gap. If it is missing, the curve does not show a tradable strategy, because it uses figures that were not yet known at the time of purchase.

## Choice of period

Even if the index, currency and method of calculation stay the same, completely different figures result depending on the period chosen. The MSCI World achieved a return of 7.71% a year net in euros from 1970 to 2025, and 8.49% from 1988 to 2025. An investor who only got in at the end of 1974, that is, after the slump in the oil crisis, achieved 9.7% up to 2025. The decade from 2000 to 2009 brought minus 3.76% a year, the decade from 2016 to 2025 plus 11.30%.

All these figures are correct and come from the same data series. Projected over thirty years, €10,000 at 8.49% becomes around €115,000, and at 11.30% around €248,000. The difference arises solely from the choice of period and not in the market. A start year immediately after a crash is the easiest way to make a strategy look good.

bloecke.titel: MSCI World return over five periods
bloecke.unter: MSCI World, net total return in DM/euros, geometric mean as a percentage a year. All values come from the same data series; only the start and end of the period differ.

bloecke.formel: g = (Final value / Start value)^(1/n) - 1     and approximately     g ≈ a - σ^2 / 2
bloecke.erklaerung: The [[geometric mean]] g is the return that actually materialises in the portfolio. The arithmetic mean a is the average of the annual values. It is always higher as soon as returns fluctuate. The gap grows roughly with half the variance, that is, with the square of the volatility.
variablen: geometric return per year, the actual rate at which the capital grows

bloecke.beispiel: For the MSCI World 1988-2025, a = 10.24% and σ = 18.77%. The approximation gives 0.1024 − 0.1877² / 2 = 0.0848, that is, 8.48%. The exactly compounded value is 8.49%.

bloecke.md: The method of calculation is the second major influence. It is noticed less often than the choice of period, because both values are correctly calculated. Only one of them, however, describes how a portfolio develops. Over 38 years, €10,000 becomes around €221,000 or around €406,000 depending on the method of calculation, almost double, even though neither figure is wrong.

bloecke.titel: Quick check of German fund offers
bloecke.md:
The first step is the key information document. Under the PRIIPs Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014, it has also existed for funds and ETFs since 2023. The performance scenarios in it are derived from historical data. They extrapolate the chosen period and are not a forecast.

Next, the cost basis is checked. In Germany, fund returns are usually reported using the **BVI method**, that is, with distributions reinvested but without the initial charge. At 6.0% a year over ten years and a 5% charge, the effective return is 5.5% a year.

Finally, the figures are converted to the after-tax level. Capital income is subject to 25% flat-rate withholding tax plus the solidarity surcharge (Section 32d(1) EStG, Income Tax Act) to the extent that it exceeds the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 (Section 20(9) EStG). For equity funds, 30% of the income is partially exempt under Section 20 InvStG (Investment Tax Act), and the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale) under Section 18 InvStG is charged on an ongoing basis. No portfolio therefore achieves an advertised gross return in full.

These distortions also affect analyses that favour passive investing. In May 2026, Cremers, Fulkerson and Riley recalculated the SPIVA analysis using three different methodological choices. They weighted by assets under management instead of equally, counted closed funds with their return up to closure instead of treating them across the board as underperformers, and compared against index funds that can be bought instead of the index itself. For US equity funds over the twenty years from 2005 to 2024, averaged across twelve categories by size and investment style, this produced around 55% underperformance instead of 92%. The 92% counts funds, while the 55% measures the assets invested. For bond funds over ten years, the conclusion is reversed, at 37% instead of 71%.

The study was funded by the Active Managers Council of the Investment Adviser Association. This conflict of interest belongs on the checklist, but it does not invalidate the study's argument. Even at 55%, the odds are only roughly even, and that is already after deducting costs, because the study compares net returns. So it too shows no advantage for active funds. A data check is only credible if your own position is subjected to the same questions.
First check the population, then the period and then the origin of the rule. For most sales documents, these three questions are enough if they are asked before looking at the figure.

mitnehmen: Over twenty years, only just over a third of active funds survive, so any analysis that does not state the population is biased upwards.
Between the data start date and the launch date of an index lie simulated values, which for smart beta indices are flattered by around three percentage points a year.
The most common look-ahead bias arises from the gap between the balance sheet date and the publication date, and a six-month gap is the standard that avoids it.
Depending on the period, the same data series gives minus 3.76% or plus 11.30% a year, and both values are correct.
The portfolio return corresponds to the geometric mean, which is approximately half the variance below the arithmetic mean.

begriffe.text: Distortion that arises when only the units still in existence are analysed. Since closed and merged funds are predominantly the weak ones, any statistic without a survivorship correction turns out systematically too good.

Distortion in which a test uses information that was not yet public at the simulated time of trading, for example balance sheet figures from the balance sheet date instead of from the publication date, or today's index composition for the past.
Fitting a strategy to random patterns in historical data by trying out many variants. The more attempts are made, the longer the data series must be for a good result to be meaningful.

The average rate of return actually achieved over several periods, calculated as the n-th root of the ratio of final value to starting value, minus 1. With fluctuating returns, it is always below the arithmetic mean, by approximately half the variance.

The method of calculating fund performance that is customary in Germany, in which distributions are treated as reinvested and the initial charge is not taken into account. The reported figure is therefore higher than what an investor paying the charge achieves.
